[[Manichaean alphabet|Manichaean script]] | notice = IPA }} '''Bactrian''' ({{langx|xbc-Grek|Αριαο|ariao|link=no}} {{IPA|xbc|arjaː||cat=no}}, meaning "Iranian"){{Cite web |last=Foundation |first=Encyclopaedia Iranica |title=Welcome to Encyclopaedia Iranica |url=https://iranicaonline.org/articles/iranian-identity-ii-pre-islamic-period/ |access-date=2023-07-31 |website=iranicaonline.org |language=en-US}} was an [[Eastern Iranian language]] formerly spoken in the [[Central Asia]]n region of [[Bactria]] (some regions of present-day Afghanistan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan){{cite web|last1=Sims-Williams|first1=N|title=Bactrian Language|url=http://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/bactrian-language|website=Encyclopaedia Iranica}} and used as the official language of the [[Kushan Empire|Kushan]] and the [[Hephthalite Empire|Hephthalite]] empires. ==Name== It was long thought that [[Avestan language|Avestan]] represented "Old Bactrian", but this notion had "rightly fallen into discredit by the end of the 19th century".{{harvnb|Gershevitch|1983|p=1250}} Bactrian, which was written predominantly in an alphabet based on the [[Greek script]], was known natively as {{lang|xbc-Grek|αριαο}} {{IPA|[arjaː]}} ("[[Arya]]"; an [[endonym]] common amongst Indo-Iranian peoples). It has also been known by names such as Greco-Bactrian or Kushan or Kushano-Bactrian. Under Kushan rule, Bactria became known as ''Tukhara'' or ''Tokhara'', and later as ''[[Tokharistan]]''. When texts in two extinct and [[Tocharian languages|previously unknown Indo-European languages]] were discovered in the [[Tarim Basin]] of China, during the early 20th century, they were linked circumstantially to Tokharistan, and Bactrian was sometimes referred to as "Eteo-Tocharian" (i.e. "true" or "original" Tocharian). By the 1970s, however, it became clear that there was little evidence for such a connection. For instance, the Tarim "Tocharian" languages were "[[centum]]" languages within the Indo-European family, whereas Bactrian was an Iranian, thus "[[satem]]" language. ==Classification== Bactrian is a part of the [[Eastern Iranian languages]] and shares features with the extinct Middle Iranian languages [[Sogdian language|Sogdian]] and [[Khwarezmian language|Khwarezmian]] (Eastern) and [[Parthian language|Parthian]] ([[Western Iranian|Western]]), as well as sharing affinity with the modern Eastern Iranian languages such as [[Pashto]] and the [[Pamir languages|Pamir]] subgroup of languages like [[Munji language|Munji]] and [[Yidgha language|Yidgha]] which are part of the same branch of the Pamir languages.Henning (1960), p. 47. ''Bactrian thus "occupies an intermediary position between Pashto and Yidgha-Munji on the one hand, Sogdian, Choresmian, and Parthian on the other: it is thus in its natural and rightful place in Bactria".'' Its genealogical position is unclear.{{cite journal|first=Ľubomir|last=Novák|title=Question of (re)classification of Eastern Iranian languages|journal=Linguistica Brunensia|year=2014|pages=77–87}} According to another source, the present-day speakers of Munji, the modern Eastern Iranian language of the Munjan Valley in the [[Kuran wa Munjan District|Kuran wa Munjan district]] of the [[Badakhshan Province|Badakhshan province]] in northeast [[Afghanistan]], display the closest possible linguistic affinity with the Bactrian language.Waghmar, Burzine K. (2001) 'Bactrian History and Language: An Overview.' Journal of the K. R. Cama Oriental Institute, 64. pp. 45. ==History== [[File:Rabatak inscription.jpg|thumb|upright=1.5|The [[Rabatak inscription]] is an inscription written on a rock in the Bactrian language and the Greek script, which was found in 1993 at the site of [[Robatak, Afghanistan|Rabatak]], near [[Surkh Kotal]] in [[Afghanistan]]. The inscription relates to the rule of the [[Kushan Empire|Kushan]] emperor [[Kanishka]], and gives remarkable clues on the genealogy of the Kushan dynasty.]] Bactrian became the [[lingua franca]] of the Kushan Empire and the region of Bactria, replacing the Greek language. Bactrian was used by successive rulers in Bactria, until the arrival of the [[Umayyad Caliphate]]. ===Historical development=== Following the conquest of Bactria by [[Alexander the Great]] in 323 BC, for about two centuries [[Greek language|Greek]] was the administrative language of his [[Hellenistic]] successors, that is, the [[Seleucid]] and the [[Greco-Bactrian kingdom]]s. Eastern [[Scythians|Scythian]] tribes (the [[Saka]], or Sacaraucae of Greek sources) invaded the territory around 140 BC, and at some time after 124 BC, Bactria was overrun by a confederation of tribes belonging to the [[Great Yuezhi]] and [[Bactria#Daxia, Tukhara and Tokharistan|''Tokhari'']]. In the 1st century AD, the Kushana, one of the Yuezhi tribes, founded the ruling dynasty of the [[Kushan Empire]]. The Kushan Empire initially retained the [[Greek language]] for administrative purposes but soon began to use Bactrian. The Bactrian [[Rabatak inscription]] (discovered in 1993 and deciphered in 2000) records that the Kushan king [[Kanishka]] ({{Circa|127 AD}})Harry Falk (2001), "The yuga of Sphujiddhvaja and the era of the Kuṣâṇas." Silk Road Art and Archaeology 7: 121–36.p. 133. discarded Greek ("Ionian") as the language of administration and adopted Bactrian ("Arya language"). The Greek language accordingly vanished from official use and only Bactrian was later attested. The [[Greek script]], however, remained and was used to write Bactrian. The territorial expansion of the Kushans helped propagate Bactrian in other parts of [[Central Asia]] and [[Pakistan|South Western Asia]]. In the 3rd century, the Kushan territories west of the [[Indus River]] fell to the [[Sassanid Empire|Sasanians]], and Bactrian began to be influenced by [[Middle Persian]]. The eastern extent of the Kushan Empire in Northwestern India, was conquered by the [[Gupta Empire]]. Besides the [[Pahlavi script]] and the [[Brahmi script]], some coinage of this period is still in the Aryo (Bactrian) script. From the mid-4th century, Bactria and northwestern India gradually fell under the control the [[Hephthalite]] and other [[Huna people|Huna tribes]]. The Hephthalite period is marked by linguistic diversity; in addition to Bactrian, Middle Persian, [[Indo-Aryan languages|Indo-Aryan]] and [[Latin]] vocabulary is also attested. The Hephthalites ruled these regions until the 7th century, when they were overrun by the [[Umayyad Caliphate]], after which official use of Bactrian ceased. Although Bactrian briefly survived in other usage, that also eventually ceased, and the latest known examples of the Bactrian script, found in the [[Tochi Valley]] in Pakistan, date to the end of the 9th century.{{cite book |title=History of Civilizations of Central Asia: The Development of Sedentary and Nomadic Civilizations, 700 B. C. to A, Part 250 |edition=illustrated |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9U6RlVVjpakC&pg=PA433 |access-date=27 March 2013 |year=1994 |publisher=[[UNESCO]] |isbn=9231028464 |page=433 }} ==Writing system== [[File:Sho uc lc 2.svg|thumb|upright=0.7|Bactrian was written using the [[Greek script]], with the addition of the letter [[Sho (letter)|sho]] (majuscule: Ϸ, minuscule: ϸ) to represent the {{IPA|/ʃ/}} sound.|class=skin-invert-image]] Among Indo-Iranian languages, the use of the Greek script is unique to Bactrian. Although ambiguities remain, some of the disadvantages were overcome by using ''[[upsilon]]'' ({{lang|xbc-Grek|Υ}}, {{lang|xbc-Grek|υ}}) for {{IPA|/h/}} and by introducing an additional 25th letter [[Sho (letter)|sho]] ({{lang|xbc-Grek|Ϸ}}, {{lang|xbc-Grek|ϸ}}) to represent {{IPA|/ʃ/}}.{{cite encyclopedia|encyclopedia=Concise encyclopedia of languages of the world|editor1-first=Keith|editor1-last=Brown|editor2-first=Sarah|editor2-last=Ogilvie|first=P. O.|last=Skjærvø|year=2009|title=Bactrian|page=115|place=Oxford|publisher=Elsevier|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=F2SRqDzB50wC&q=Bactrian+Kaniska+letter&pg=PA115|isbn=9780080877754}} ''[[Xi (letter)|Xi]]'' ({{lang|xbc-Grek|Ξ}}, {{lang|xbc-Grek|ξ}}) and ''[[Psi (letter)|psi]]'' ({{lang|xbc-Grek|Ψ}}, {{lang|xbc-Grek|ψ}}) were not used for writing Bactrian as the ''ks'' and ''ps'' sequences did not occur in Bactrian.{{Cite book |title=History of Civilizations of Central Asia |publisher=UNESCO |year=2006 |isbn=978-9231032110 |pages=121}} They were, however, probably used to represent numbers (just as other Greek letters were). The Greek writing reproduced the Bactrian phonetics only approximately.{{Cite book |title=History of Civilizations of Central Asia |publisher=UNESCO |year=2006 |isbn=978-9231032110 |pages=121}} ===Records=== [[File:Alchono legend with coin.jpg|thumb|The word {{lang|xbc-Grek|αλχοννο}} ({{transliteration|xbc|alkhonno}}) in cursive Bactrian script, on a coin of the [[Alchon Huns]] ruler [[Khingila]], 5th century AD.[[File:Khingila Alchono inscription.jpg|30px]][[Khingila]] with the word "{{Transliteration|xbc|Alchono}}" in the [[Bactrian script]] ({{lang|xbc-Grek|αλχονο}}) and the [[Tamgha]] symbol on his coins [https://www.cngcoins.com/Coin.aspx?CoinID=114833 CNG Coins].{{cite book |last1=Alemany |first1=Agustí |title=Sources on the Alans: A Critical Compilation |date=2000 |publisher=BRILL |isbn=9004114424 |page=346 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8bZ4c5oZpNAC&pg=PA346 |language=en}}[https://www.cngcoins.com/Coin.aspx?CoinID=90023 CNG Coins]]] The Bactrian language is known from inscriptions, coins, seals, manuscripts, and other documents. Sites at which Bactrian language inscriptions have been found are (in north–south order) [[Afrasiyab (Samarkand)|Afrasiyab]] in [[Uzbekistan]]; [[Termez|Kara-Tepe]], Airtam, [[Delbarjin]], [[Balkh]], [[Kunduz]], [[Baghlan|Baglan]], [[Surkh Kotal|Ratabak/Surkh Kotal]], [[Oruzgan]], [[Kabul]], Dasht-e Navur, [[Ghazni]], Jagatu in [[Afghanistan]]; and [[Islamabad]], [[Shatial|Shatial Bridge]] and [[Tochi Valley]] in [[Pakistan]]. {{sfn|Chisholm|1911}} Of eight known manuscript fragments in Greco-Bactrian script, one is from [[Loulan|Lou-lan]] and seven from Toyoq, where they were discovered by the second and third [[Turpan]] expeditions under [[Albert von Le Coq]]. One of these may be a [[Buddhist]] text. One other manuscript, in [[Manichaean alphabet|Manichaean script]], was found at [[Gaochang|Qočo]] by [[Mary Boyce]] in 1958. Over 150 legal documents, accounts, letters and Buddhist texts have surfaced since the 1990s, the largest collection of which is the [[Khalili Collection of Aramaic Documents]].{{Cite journal|last=Gholami|first=Saloumeh|date=2013|title=Review of Bactrian Documents from Northern Afghanistan. III: Plates. Studies in the Khalili Collection, Vol. 3. CIIr. Pt. 2, Inscriptions of the Seleucid and Parthian Periods and of Eastern Iran and Central Asia. Vol. 4, Bactrian|url=http://www.jstor.org/stable/43307651|journal=Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society|volume=23|issue=1|pages=136–138|jstor=43307651|issn=1356-1863}} These have greatly increased the detail in which Bactrian is currently known.{{Cite journal|last=Sims-Williams|first=Nicholas|author-link=Nicholas Sims-Williams|date=March 2002|title=New Documents in Ancient Bactrian Reveal Afghanistan's Past|url=https://www.iias.asia/sites/default/files/nwl_article/2019-11/IIAS_NL27_1213.pdf|journal=IIAS Newsletter|publisher=International Institute for Asian Studies|issue=27|pages=12–13}} ==Phonology== [[File:Surkh Kotal inscription, 2nd century CE.jpg|thumb|upright=1.5|The [[Surkh Kotal]] inscription (SK4) is the first known substantial document written in Bactrian, an Iranian language. It uses the [[Greek script]]. It was written at the time of the [[Kushan Empire|Kushan]] ruler [[Huvishka]], 2nd century CE. [[Kabul Museum]].{{cite book |last1=Nakamura |first1=Hajime |title=Indian Buddhism: A Survey with Bibliographical Notes |date=1987 |publisher=Motilal Banarsidass Publ. |isbn=978-81-208-0272-8 |page=141, note 2 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=w0A7y4TCeVQC&pg=PA141 |language=en}}]] The phonology of Bactrian is not known with certainty, owing to the limitations of the native scripts, and also its status as an extinct language. ===Consonants=== {| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center" |+ Consonants of Bactrian |- !colspan="2" rowspan="2"| Type !rowspan="2"| [[Labial consonant|Labial]] !rowspan="2"| [[Dental consonant|Dental]] or

Here, their [[endonym]] {{lang|xbc-Grek|ηβοδαλο}} ({{Transliteration|xbc|ēbodalo}}), "[[Hephthalites]]".|class=skin-invert-image]] A major difficulty in determining Bactrian phonology is that affricates and voiced stops were not consistently distinguished from the corresponding fricatives in the Greek script. * [[Proto-Iranian]] *b, *d, *g have generally become spirants, as in most other Eastern Iranian languages. A distinctive feature of Bactrian, shared within the Iranian languages with Munji, Yidgha and Pashto, is the development of Proto-Iranian *d > *ð further to {{IPA|/l/}}, which may have been areal in nature. Original *d remains only in a few consonant clusters, e.g. *bandaka > {{lang|xbc-Grek|βανδαγο}} 'servant', *dugdā > {{lang|xbc-Grek|λογδο}} 'daughter'. The clusters {{IPA|/lr/}} and {{IPA|/rl/}} appear in earlier Bactrian, but revert to {{IPA|/dr/}}, {{IPA|/rd/}} later, e.g. *drauga > {{lang|xbc-Grek|λρωγο}} (4th to 5th century) > {{lang|xbc-Grek|δδρωρο}} (7th to 8th century) 'lie, falsehood'.{{sfn|Gholami|2010|pp=18–19}} * Proto-Iranian *p, *t, *č, *k have become voiced between vowels, and after a nasal consonant or *r. ** Inside a word, the digraphs {{lang|xbc-Grek|ββ}}, {{lang|xbc-Grek|δδ}} for original voiceless *p, *t can be found, which probably represent {{IPA|[b]}}, {{IPA|[d]}}. The former is attested only in a single word, {{lang|xbc-Grek|αββο}} 'water'. Manichaean Bactrian appears to only have had {{IPA|/v/}} in native vocabulary. According to Gholami, instances of single {{lang|xbc-Grek|δ}} may indicate a fricative pronunciation, {{IPA|[ð]}}.{{sfn|Gholami|2010|p=10}} ** {{lang|xbc-Grek|γ}} appears to stand for both the stop {{IPA|[ɡ]}} and the fricative {{IPA|[ɣ]}}, but it is unclear if a contrast existed, and which instances are which. Evidence from the Manichaean script suggests that {{lang|xbc-Grek|γ}} from *k may have been {{IPA|/ɡ/}} and {{lang|xbc-Grek|γ}} from *g may have been {{IPA|/ɣ/}}. According to Greek orthographic practices, {{lang|xbc-Grek|γγ}} represents {{IPA|[ŋɡ]}}.{{sfn|Gholami|2010|pp=11–12}} * {{lang|xbc-Grek|σ}} may continue both Proto-Iranian *c > *s and *č, and the Manichaean script confirms that it represents two phonemes, likely {{IPA|/s/}} and {{IPA|/ts/}}.{{sfn|Gholami|2010|p=12}} * {{lang|xbc-Grek|ζ}} may continue similarly on one hand Proto-Iranian *dz > *z, and on the other *ǰ and *č, and it represents at least {{IPA|/z/}} and {{IPA|/dz/}}. This distinction is again confirmed by the Manichaean script. Also a third counterpart of {{lang|xbc-Grek|ζ}} is found in Manichaean Bactrian, possibly representing {{IPA|/ʒ/}}. The status of {{lang|xbc-Grek|θ}} is unclear; it only appears in the word {{lang|xbc-Grek|ιθαο}} 'thus, also', which may be a loanword from another Iranian language. In most positions Proto-Iranian *θ becomes {{IPA|/h/}} (written {{lang|xbc-Grek|υ}}), or is lost, e.g. *puθra- > {{lang|xbc-Grek|πουρο}} 'son'.{{sfn|Gholami|2010|p=13}} The cluster *θw, however, appears to become {{IPA|/lf/}}, e.g. *wikāθwan > {{lang|xbc-Grek|οιγαλφο}} 'witness'.{{sfn|Gholami|2010|p=25}} {{lang|xbc-Grek|ϸ}} continues, in addition to Proto-Iranian *š, also Proto-Iranian *s in the clusters *sr, *str, *rst. In several cases, however, Proto-Iranian *š becomes {{IPA|/h/}} or is lost; the distribution is unclear. E.g. *snušā > {{lang|xbc-Grek|ασνωυο}} 'daughter-in-law', *aštā > {{lang|xbc-Grek|αταο}} 'eight', *xšāθriya > {{lang|xbc-Grek|χαρο}} 'ruler', *pašman- > {{lang|xbc-Grek|παμανο}} 'wool'. ===Vowels=== {| |+ '''Vowels of Bactrian''' |- | {| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center" |- !rowspan="2"| Type !! colspan="3"| Short |- ! Bactrian script legend: {{lang|xbc-Grek|χιγγιλο αλχοννο}} {{transliteration|xbc|khingilo alkhonno}}, with Alchon [[tamgha]] symbol [[File:Alchon_Tamga.png|15px|class=skin-invert]].This coin is in the collection of the [[British Museum]]. For equivalent coin, see [https://www.cngcoins.com/Coin.aspx?CoinID=156854 CNG Coins]]] The Greek script does not consistently represent vowel length. Fewer vowel contrasts yet are found in the Manichaean script, but short {{IPA|/a/}} and long {{IPA|/aː/}} are distinguished in it, suggesting that Bactrian generally retains the Proto-Iranian vowel length contrast. It is not clear if {{lang|xbc-Grek|ο}} might represent short {{IPA|[o]}} in addition to {{IPA|[u]}}, and if any contrast existed. Short {{IPA|[o]}} may have occurred at least as a reflex of *a followed by a lost *u in the next syllable, e.g. *madu > {{lang|xbc-Grek|μολο}} 'wine', *pasu > {{lang|xbc-Grek|ποσο}} 'sheep'. Short {{IPA|[e]}} is also rare. By contrast, long {{IPA|/eː/}}, {{IPA|/oː/}} are well established as reflexes of Proto-Iranian diphthongs and certain vowel-semivowel sequences: {{lang|xbc-Grek|η}} < *ai, *aya, *iya; {{lang|xbc-Grek|ω}} < *au, *awa. An epenthetic vowel {{IPA|[ə]}} (written {{lang|xbc-Grek|α}}) is inserted before word-initial [[consonant cluster]]s. Original word-final vowels and word-initial vowels in open syllables were generally lost. A word-final {{lang|xbc-Grek|ο}} is normally written, but this was probably silent, and it is appended even after retained word-final vowels: e.g. *aštā > {{lang|xbc-Grek|αταο}} 'eight', likely pronounced {{IPA|/ataː/}}. The Proto-Iranian syllabic rhotic *r̥ is lost in Bactrian, and is reflected as {{lang|xbc-Grek|ορ}} adjacent to labial consonants, {{lang|xbc-Grek|ιρ}} elsewhere; this agrees with the development in the western Iranian languages [[Parthian language|Parthian]] and [[Middle Persian]]. ===Orthography=== [[File:Kushan script.jpg|thumb|upright=1.7|Variations of the [[Greek alphabet]] (narrow columns) in the [[Kushan script|Kushan]] script (wide columns).|class=skin-invert-image]] {| class="wikitable" |+ Letter correspondence !
